pandas - Missing Data, Reshape & Speed
5. Missing Values
Four different nulls, and none of them equals itself.

items: Always test with .isna(), never with == np.nan.

blocks.text: 7. apply vs Vectorized
apply(axis=1) builds a Series per row. It is a Python loop wearing a pandas coat.

items: Two branches -> np.where. Many branches -> np.select.
Lookup by key -> .map(dict) or a merge, not apply.
String work -> .str accessor, which is already vectorized.

Never grow a frame in a loop; collect rows, concat once.

Copy-on-write (pandas 3.x) makes chained assignment an error, not a warning.

blocks.text: PySpark - Execution Model
1. DataFrame vs RDD
Both are distributed collections. Only one of them gets optimised.

items: DataFrame: use it unless you have a reason not to.
RDD: custom partitioners, non-tabular data, low-level control.
Python UDFs break Catalyst's view - prefer built-in functions.

blocks.text: 2. Lazy Evaluation
Transformations build a plan. Nothing executes until an action asks for a result.

items: Plan stages: parsed -> analyzed -> optimized -> physical -> RDDs.
df.explain(True) prints all four.
Errors in a typo'd column surface at analysis, not at write.

blocks.text: 3. Transformations vs Actions
If it returns a DataFrame it is lazy. If it returns data, a number, or writes files, it runs.

items.text: - select, filter, withColumn - no data movement.

blocks.text: 4. Job / Stage / Task
The unit you tune is the task; the unit you read in the UI is the stage.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text:
collect() and toPandas() pull every row to the driver - OOM at scale.
cache() is a transformation: it does nothing until the next action.

blocks.caption: One task per partition, per stage

blocks.text: PySpark - Shuffle, Partitions & Caching
5. Shuffle
A shuffle redistributes rows across partitions by key. It writes to disk, crosses the network, and ends a stage.

items: Triggered by groupBy, join, distinct, orderBy, repartition.
spark.sql.shuffle.partitions defaults to 200 - often wrong both ways.
Broadcast the small side of a join to avoid the shuffle entirely.

blocks.text: 6. Partitions
Partitions are the unit of parallelism. Aim for 100-200 MB each and a multiple of your total cores.

items.text: - full shuffle, up or down, rebalances.
- no shuffle, down only, may leave skew.

items: Partition on write by a low-cardinality column, never by an id.

blocks.text: 7. cache / persist
Caching pays off only when a DataFrame is reused. Otherwise it is memory you took from the shuffle.

items: cache() = persist(MEMORY_AND_DISK) for DataFrames.
Lazy: the first action materialises it.
unpersist() when done - cached blocks evict live ones.

blocks.text: 8. Tuning Checklist

items: Read the SQL tab: find the widest stage, not the slowest line.
Filter and select before the join, not after.
Enable AQE - it coalesces partitions and handles skewed joins.
Check the max/median task time ratio: > 3 means skew.

blocks.code:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", 400)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", True)

blocks.text:
Caching a DataFrame used once is pure overhead.
Caching before a filter caches the unfiltered rows too.

blocks.text: SQL - Query Logic, Grouping & Joins
1. Logical Query Order
You write SELECT first. The engine runs it almost last. Most SQL traps follow from this one fact.

items: SELECT aliases are not visible to WHERE or GROUP BY.
WHERE cannot see aggregates. HAVING can.
ORDER BY runs last, so it can use SELECT aliases.

blocks.text: 2. WHERE vs HAVING
Same keyword family, different stage of the pipeline.
3. GROUP BY Grain
The grain is the column set in GROUP BY: one output row per distinct combination. Change the grain and every aggregate changes.

items: Every non-aggregated SELECT column must appear in GROUP BY.

blocks.text: 4. JOIN Types
Pick the join by which side you must keep, then check the key's uniqueness.

items: A join on a non-unique key multiplies rows (fan-out).
Aggregate first, then join - never the reverse.
Anti-join: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.id IS NULL or NOT EXISTS.

blocks.code:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM emp
WHERE hired >= '2024-01-01'  -- rows
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;        -- groups
blocks.title: Example - grouped query
Common trap
blocks.text:
HAVING with no GROUP BY treats the whole result as one group.
A row filter in HAVING still works, but scans far more rows.

blocks.code:
-- grain = (dept): 1 row per dept
-- grain = (dept, month): 1 per dept-month
SELECT dept, DATE_TRUNC('month', d) AS m,
       SUM(amt) AS total,
       COUNT(DISTINCT emp_id) AS people
FROM sales GROUP BY 1, 2;
blocks.title: Example - changing the grain
Common trap
blocks.text:
JOIN before GROUP BY fans out rows and inflates SUM.
Symptom: totals that are an exact multiple of the truth.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text:
LEFT JOIN ... WHERE b.col = 'x' silently becomes an INNER JOIN.
Filter the right table in ON; filter the left table in WHERE.
SQL - Window Functions & CTEs
5. Window Function Anatomy
A window function adds a column computed over related rows. It never removes rows - that is the whole difference from GROUP BY.

items.text: - defines row order inside the partition.
- picks which rows feed the aggregate.

blocks.text: 6. Ranking Family
All four differ only in how they treat ties.

items: Deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER() ... = 1, never with RANK().
Add a tiebreaker column to make ROW_NUMBER deterministic.

blocks.text: 7. LAG / LEAD
Reach into the previous or next row of the same partition - the standard way to compute deltas and gaps.

items.text: - offset then default; default is NULL.

items: The OVER's ORDER BY is independent of the query's ORDER BY.

blocks.text: 8. CTEs
A CTE names a step. It is readability first, and the only clean way to filter on a window result.

items: A CTE is not a guarantee of materialization - plans may inline it.
Recursive: WITH RECURSIVE in Postgres, plain WITH in SQL Server.

blocks.code:
SUM(amount) OVER (
  PARTITION BY cust_id
  ORDER BY order_date
  ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
) AS rolling_3
blocks.title: Example - OVER(...)
Important
blocks.text:
Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING - a running total.
RANGE groups peer rows with equal ORDER BY values; ROWS counts physical rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT d, v,
  LAG(v) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY d) AS prev,
  v - LAG(v) OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY d) AS delta
FROM readings;
blocks.title: Example - previous observed value

blocks.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY cust_id
    ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
blocks.title: Example - latest row per key
Common trap
blocks.text:
You cannot put a window function in WHERE - it has not been computed yet.
Wrap it in a CTE (or subquery) and filter outside.

page.title: Dictionary pattern C - Latest record per entity
page.summary: Coding / Python / Dictionaries / Grouping and state

children.text: Keep the latest record for each entity_id. Input is not sorted. updated_at values are comparable timestamps in one time basis. On equal timestamps, keep the last input record.

items: Choose entity_id as key.
Store the first record for an unseen key.
Compare candidate and stored timestamps.
Use >= to implement the stated last-input-wins tie rule.

children.text: The dictionary stores the best record seen so far for each key. Update only when the candidate wins under the defined timestamp and tie policy. The sample uses numeric timestamps; arbitrary date strings must be parsed and normalized before comparison.
Stable sorting then overwriting gives the same tie behavior, but costs O(n log n) time and O(n) temporary storage.
Single pass: expected O(n) time and O(k) retained references for k entities. Missing or incomparable timestamps require an explicit validation policy.

page.summary: Hybrid / Data Modeling / Join grain / Slowly changing dimensions

children.text: An orders-to-customer-history join doubles revenue. What would you inspect and how would you demonstrate the problem?

items: Declare the order and dimension grains.
Count dimension matches per order before summing.
Check uniqueness, current-row rules or effective-date intervals.
Compare row counts and revenue totals against the fact-only baseline.

children.text: An order may match multiple historical dimension rows. Check the dimension key and the intended as-of relationship before changing the aggregate. If the history contains overlapping effective periods, even an as-of predicate can remain non-unique.

children.code:
SELECT o.order_id, COUNT(d.customer_id) AS dimension_matches
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN customer_history AS d
  ON d.customer_id = o.customer_id
 AND o.order_date >= d.valid_from
 AND (o.order_date < d.valid_to OR d.valid_to IS NULL)
GROUP BY o.order_id
HAVING COUNT(d.customer_id) > 1;

page.title: Q1 - WHERE / GROUP BY / HAVING
page.summary: SQL / SQL / Aggregation / Row filters and group filters

children.text: Classic SQL screener: filter to PAID orders in 2026 and return total net_amount per customer. What clauses do you need, and what is the output grain?

items: State the input grain: one row per order.
Use WHERE for status and the year interval.
GROUP BY customer_id and SUM net_amount.
For the follow-up, apply HAVING SUM(net_amount) > 1000.

children.text: Filter order rows first, then aggregate. The output has one row per customer with qualifying orders. A revenue threshold belongs in HAVING after grouping. This example uses PostgreSQL-style DATE literals, a half-open date interval and non-null net_amount.

children.code:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(net_amount) AS total_paid_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID'
  AND order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date < DATE '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id;

children.text: For the follow-up, add HAVING after GROUP BY. A grouped CTE followed by an outer WHERE is another readable composition.

children.code:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(net_amount) AS total_paid_revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID'
  AND order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND order_date < DATE '2027-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(net_amount) > 1000;

children.text: Filtering a row amount above 1000 is not the same as retaining a customer whose aggregate exceeds 1000.

items: How would you keep only customers whose total paid revenue exceeds 1000?
WHERE filters rows.
GROUP BY changes the output grain.
HAVING filters aggregated groups.

page.title: Q2 - LEFT JOIN and revenue grain
page.summary: SQL / SQL / Joins / Cardinality and preservation

children.text: Classic SQL screener: return total paid revenue for every customer, including customers with no paid orders. Which join do you use and where should the paid-order filter go?

items: Confirm customers.customer_id is unique.
Preserve customers with LEFT JOIN.
Restrict matching orders in ON, not an outer WHERE.
Check dimension cardinality and revenue totals before and after any additional join.

children.text: Start from the unique customer table and LEFT JOIN matching paid orders. Put the paid-order predicate in ON to preserve customers without a match. COALESCE turns their null total into zero. Check the relationship grain before summing.

children.code:
SELECT c.customer_id, COALESCE(SUM(o.net_amount), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
 AND o.status = 'PAID'
GROUP BY c.customer_id;

children.text: Pre-aggregate paid orders to one row per customer before the LEFT JOIN. A later non-unique dimension join can still multiply those totals; fix its key or effective-date condition.

children.title: Watch for this
children.text: A WHERE o.status = PAID condition removes the null-extended rows. SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a general repair for fan-out: different orders can have equal amounts.

items: What happens if one customer has multiple matching dimension rows before you SUM revenue?
LEFT JOIN preservation.
Predicate placement.
Join cardinality.

page.title: Q4 - Aggregate, then rank with a CTE

children.text: Classic SQL screener: when a problem needs aggregation followed by ranking/filtering, why might you use a CTE, and is a CTE automatically faster than a subquery?

children.text: A CTE names an intermediate result and exposes its grain. First produce customer-level revenue, then rank that result. WITH does not itself promise a speedup: optimization and materialization depend on the engine, query and references.

children.code:
WITH revenue AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(net_amount) AS total_revenue
  FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID'
  GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, total_revenue,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_revenue DESC) AS revenue_rank
FROM revenue
ORDER BY revenue_rank, customer_id;

page.title: Q5 - Previous observed row: LAG or self-join

children.text: Classic SQL screener: how can a self-join reproduce previous/next-row logic, when would you prefer LAG/LEAD, and how would you respond if the interviewer restricts available SQL features?

items: Define partition, order and uniqueness.
Use LAG within each account for the previous observed value.
Without windows, match the maximum earlier date.
Retain the first row with a null predecessor and explain query-plan tradeoffs.

children.text: Clarify previous observed balance rather than previous calendar day. Assume one row per (account_id, observed_date). LAG expresses adjacency directly. Without windows, choose the greatest earlier observed date, then join that row. Duplicate dates require a stable tie-breaker in both approaches.
No window functions: the uniqueness assumption makes the predecessor join return at most one row. An index beginning with (account_id, observed_date) may help; inspect the real plan.

children.code:
SELECT b.account_id, b.observed_date, b.balance,
       p.balance AS previous_balance
FROM balances AS b
LEFT JOIN balances AS p
  ON p.account_id = b.account_id
 AND p.observed_date = (
   SELECT MAX(x.observed_date)
   FROM balances AS x
   WHERE x.account_id = b.account_id
     AND x.observed_date < b.observed_date
 );

children.title: Watch for this
children.text: A self-join on previous.date < current.date alone returns all earlier rows and multiplies the output. Subtracting one day misses gaps in observations.

page.title: Cache and persistence

# Run in an existing SparkSession named spark; bounded toy data.
base = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("NO", True), ("NO", False), ("CH", True)],
    ["country", "is_active"],
).filter("country IS NOT NULL").persist()
try:
    base.count()  # materialize intentionally for this demonstration
    by_country = base.groupBy("country").count()
    active_rows = base.filter("is_active")
    by_country.show()   # action while the cached base is retained
    active_rows.show()  # another action before release
finally:
    base.unpersist()
# Do not cache every DataFrame in production; measure actual reuse and cost.

page.title: Inner, left and anti joins
page.summary: Choose join semantics from the question, not from habit.

blocks.text: Choose join semantics from the question, not from habit.

items: INNER keeps only matching rows.
LEFT keeps every left row and adds nullable right columns.
LEFT ANTI (or NOT EXISTS) finds left rows without a match.

blocks.title: Example
LEFT JOIN: right-side filters belong in ON
blocks.code:
-- Keeps every customer; only orders from 2026 are matched.
SELECT c.customer_id, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
  AND o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01';

-- The same predicate in WHERE removes customers without a 2026 order,
-- because o.order_date IS NULL for them: the query now behaves like an INNER JOIN.

blocks.code:
SELECT c.customer_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL;  -- NULL here only when nothing matched

blocks.title: Worked example: pass, then fail loudly
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3], "customer_id": [10, 10, 20]})
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [10, 20, 30], "country": ["NO", "CH", "NO"]})

joined = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left",
                      validate="many_to_one", indicator=True)
print(len(orders), len(joined))            # 3 3: the order grain is kept
print(joined["_merge"].value_counts())     # all "both": no unmatched orders

duplicated = pd.concat([customers, customers.iloc[[0]]])  # customer 10 twice
try:
    orders.merge(duplicated, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError as err:
    print("cardinality violated:", err)
blocks.explanation: validate checks key uniqueness only. It does not report unmatched keys (use indicator=True) and does not fix dtype mismatches. Bounded toy data; not executed during preparation.

questions.prompt: orders has one row per order and a shipping_fee column; order_lines has one row per order line. Every order has at least one line. You INNER JOIN them on order_id and compute SUM(o.shipping_fee). What happens?

options.text: The total is correct because each order is joined once.
options.explanation: Each order is repeated once per line after the join.

options.text: The shipping fee is counted once per order line, so orders with several lines are over-counted.
The query fails because the grains differ.
options.explanation: SQL does not check grain; the query runs and silently returns an inflated sum.

options.text: Orders are removed by the join.
options.explanation: Every order has at least one line, so no order disappears here.

questions.explanation: The join changes the grain to one row per order line, so order-level measures repeat (fan-out). Sum shipping_fee from orders alone, or aggregate lines to order grain before joining.

options.text: One row per order.
One row per customer that has at least one order.
One row per customer in the customers table.
options.explanation: customers is not read; customers without orders are absent.

options.text: One row per order line.

questions.explanation: GROUP BY customer_id collapses orders to one row per customer_id present in orders. To include customers without orders, start from customers and LEFT JOIN the aggregated orders.

questions.prompt: orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one") raises pandas.errors.MergeError. What does that tell you?

options.text: orders contains repeated customer_id values.
options.explanation: Repeated keys on the left are allowed: that is the "many" side.

options.text: customers contains repeated customer_id values.
Some orders have no matching customer.
options.explanation: Unmatched keys are allowed in a left merge; audit them with indicator=True.

options.text: The key columns have different dtypes.
options.explanation: validate only checks key uniqueness; dtype problems surface differently.

questions.explanation: many_to_one requires the right-hand keys to be unique, which guarantees that a left merge keeps exactly one output row per left row.

questions.prompt: Which queries return the customers that have no orders? Select all that apply.

options.text: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.customer_id IS NULL
options.explanation: An inner join keeps only matched rows, whose join key cannot be NULL: this returns nothing.

options.text: SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders), where orders.customer_id can be NULL
options.explanation: If the subquery yields a NULL, NOT IN is never true and the query returns no rows.

questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL are both anti joins. NOT IN is only safe when the subquery column cannot be NULL.

links.label: Review: inner, left and anti joins

questions.prompt: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.status = 'PAID'. What is the effect of the WHERE clause?

options.text: Every customer is still returned.
Customers without a PAID order are removed, so the query behaves like an INNER JOIN with that filter.
It is a syntax error to filter a right-side column after a LEFT JOIN.
Only customers without orders are returned.

questions.explanation: Unmatched customers have o.status = NULL, and NULL = 'PAID' is not true, so WHERE removes them. Move the predicate into ON to keep every customer.

links.label: Review: inner, left and anti joins

questions.prompt: What is the essential difference between SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) and SUM(amount) with GROUP BY customer_id?

options.text: The window version keeps one output row per input row; GROUP BY returns one row per customer.
The window version is always faster.
options.explanation: Performance depends on the engine and plan; the semantic difference is the output grain.

options.text: GROUP BY cannot be combined with SUM.
The window version counts NULL amounts as zero.
options.explanation: SUM ignores NULL inputs in both forms.

questions.explanation: A window function computes over related rows without collapsing them; GROUP BY changes the output grain.

questions.prompt: You keep ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) = 1 as the latest event. Two events of one customer share the latest event_ts. What is true?

options.text: The row inserted first is always kept.
Which of the two rows is kept is not guaranteed; add a tie-breaker such as event_id DESC.
Both rows get rn = 1.
options.explanation: That describes RANK(), not ROW_NUMBER().

options.text: The query fails because of the tie.

questions.explanation: ROW_NUMBER always assigns distinct numbers, but with tied ORDER BY values the assignment is arbitrary and can change between runs. A deterministic tie-breaker makes deduplication reproducible.

questions.prompt: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY event_ts) has no explicit frame. Two rows share the same event_ts. In PostgreSQL or Spark SQL, what do those two rows show?

options.text: The same running total, which already includes both rows.
Different running totals, increasing row by row.
options.explanation: That requires an explicit ROWS frame and a tie-breaker.

options.text: An error, because the frame is missing.
NULL for the second row.

questions.explanation: The implicit frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so peer rows with equal ORDER BY values are included together. Write ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW with a tie-breaker for a row-by-row total.

links.label: Review: ROWS versus RANGE window frames

questions.prompt: df is an existing DataFrame. You run df2 = df.filter("amount > 0").select("customer_id", "amount") and nothing else. What has Spark executed on the cluster for these two calls?

options.text: Nothing yet: the calls only extend the logical plan; work starts when an action such as count(), show() or a write runs.
A full scan of df to apply the filter.
options.explanation: filter and select are transformations; they are evaluated lazily.

options.text: One job per transformation, so two jobs.
options.explanation: Jobs are started by actions, not by transformations.

options.text: A cached copy of df2 in executor memory.
options.explanation: Nothing is cached unless you call cache()/persist() and an action then computes the data.

df.groupBy("country").agg(F.sum("amount"))

questions.prompt: Which operation normally requires a shuffle?

options.text: events.filter("amount > 0")
options.explanation: Narrow: each partition is filtered independently.

options.text: events.withColumn("amount_eur", F.col("amount") * 0.9)
options.explanation: Narrow: a per-row expression.

options.text: events.groupBy("customer_id").count()
events.coalesce(10)
options.explanation: coalesce merges existing partitions without a full shuffle by default.

questions.explanation: Grouping needs every row of a key in the same partition, so rows move across the cluster: a wide transformation with an Exchange in the plan and a stage boundary.

questions.prompt: After a selective filter you have 2,000 small partitions and want about 50 output files, without paying for a full shuffle. What is the usual choice, and its trade-off?

options.text: coalesce(50): it merges partitions without a full shuffle, but the preceding narrow work in the same stage then also runs with only 50 tasks.
repartition(50): it never shuffles.
options.explanation: repartition always performs a full shuffle; that can be worth it when you need balanced partitions.

options.text: cache() first, then write.
options.explanation: Caching does not change the number of partitions.

options.text: coalesce(1), because one file is always easiest downstream.
options.explanation: A single task writes everything: no parallelism and a bottleneck for large data.

questions.explanation: coalesce is a narrow operation that reduces partition count cheaply; because it is narrow it can also reduce the parallelism of upstream work. repartition shuffles but produces evenly sized partitions.

questions.prompt: facts is about 2 TB and dim is about 20 MB. You write facts.join(F.broadcast(dim), "product_id", "left"). What is the main effect?

options.text: A full copy of dim is sent to each executor, so the large facts side can be joined without being shuffled for this join.
facts is broadcast to every executor.
options.explanation: The hint names dim; broadcasting 2 TB would be infeasible.

options.text: The whole query is guaranteed to contain no shuffle.
options.explanation: Other operations such as a later groupBy can still shuffle.

options.text: The join result can now contain fewer rows than facts.
options.explanation: A left join keeps every facts row; the strategy does not change semantics.

questions.explanation: A broadcast hash join avoids shuffling the large side when the other side is genuinely small. Always confirm the chosen strategy in the physical plan.

questions.prompt: In a 200-task stage, one task runs for 40 minutes while the others finish in about a minute; its shuffle read is about 30 times the median. Which first steps are reasonable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Count rows per join/group key, including NULL, empty and default values.
Check whether AQE skew-join handling is enabled and applies to this join.
Double the cluster size immediately.
options.explanation: More executors do not split one oversized partition; the hot task stays slow.

options.text: coalesce the input to a single partition to even out the work.
options.explanation: That removes parallelism entirely.

questions.explanation: The symptom is data skew. Confirm the hot keys first, then consider AQE skew handling, filtering or separating the hot keys, or salting as a targeted technique.

questions.prompt: Which statement about df.cache() on a DataFrame is correct?

options.text: It computes and stores df immediately.
options.explanation: cache() is lazy.

options.text: It marks df for caching; partitions are stored when an action first computes them, and later actions can reuse them until unpersist() or eviction.
It writes df to durable storage that survives a cluster restart.
options.explanation: The cache lives in executor memory/local disk; use a table or files for durability.

options.text: It speeds up every job that uses df, even if df is used only once.
options.explanation: Without reuse, caching only adds memory pressure and materialization cost.

questions.explanation: Cache reused, expensive intermediate results; release them with unpersist() once the dependent actions have run.

questions.prompt: What can Adaptive Query Execution change at runtime in Spark SQL? Select all that apply.

options.text: Coalesce many small post-shuffle partitions into fewer ones.
Switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join when runtime statistics show one side is small enough.
Split skewed partitions in a sort-merge join.
Remove duplicated rows produced by joining at the wrong grain.
options.explanation: AQE changes the physical execution, never the result of the query.

questions.explanation: AQE re-optimizes at shuffle boundaries using measured sizes. Correctness problems such as fan-out must be fixed in the query itself.

page.title: ROWS versus RANGE window frames
page.summary: Understand window frames before relying on running or moving aggregates.

blocks.text: Understand window frames before relying on running or moving aggregates.

items: ROWS counts physical ordered rows.
RANGE groups peers with the same ordering value and can include multiple rows at once.
Always make the intended frame explicit in interview or production-critical queries.
Duplicates in the ORDER BY column are where ROWS and RANGE often diverge.

blocks.code:
SUM(amount) OVER (
  PARTITION BY account_id
  ORDER BY event_ts
  ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
)
blocks.title: Example
The implicit frame is RANGE
blocks.text: With ORDER BY and no explicit frame, PostgreSQL and Spark SQL use RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. Rows that tie on the ORDER BY value are peers and enter the running total together. Check your engine documentation before relying on a default.

blocks.title: Both frames side by side
blocks.code:
SELECT account_id, event_id, event_ts, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY account_id
         ORDER BY event_ts, event_id
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_rows,
       SUM(amount) OVER (
         PARTITION BY account_id
         ORDER BY event_ts
         RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS running_range
FROM account_events;
blocks.explanation: running_rows grows row by row thanks to the event_id tie-breaker; running_range gives both 09:00 peers the same value. Illustrative schema; not executed during preparation.

page.title: SQL grain before joins
page.summary: State the row grain of every relation before joining; most duplicate-row bugs are grain mismatches.

blocks.text: State the row grain of every relation before joining; most duplicate-row bugs are grain mismatches.

items: Ask: what does one row represent before and after each transformation?
A one-to-many join legitimately multiplies rows; it is not automatically a bug.
Aggregate to the target grain before joining when downstream metrics assume one row per key.
Validate cardinality with counts and distinct-key checks.

blocks.title: Example
Aggregate to the target grain, then join
blocks.code:
-- Target grain: one row per customer.
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)      AS order_count,
         SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price)  AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_lines l ON l.order_id = o.order_id
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id,
       c.country,
       COALESCE(t.order_count, 0) AS order_count,
       COALESCE(t.revenue, 0)     AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN order_totals t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id;
blocks.explanation: order_totals is already one row per customer, so the LEFT JOIN cannot multiply customers. COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) is needed because the inner join to order_lines is at line grain. Illustrative schema; not executed during preparation.

SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS rows_per_key
FROM customers
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

page.summary: Use windows when you need group-aware calculations while retaining row-level detail.

blocks.text: A window keeps the input grain: every input row stays in the output. GROUP BY collapses rows to the grouping grain. terms.label: MapReduce
terms.definition: The guide contrasts a disk-backed map/shuffle/reduce workflow with Spark's longer computation pipeline.

terms.label: In-memory processing
terms.definition: Spark can retain intermediate data in memory; the opening diagram uses this to explain the motivation for moving beyond repeated disk round trips.

terms.label: DAG
terms.definition: A directed acyclic graph represents the ordered work. This guide connects the graph to jobs, stages and tasks.

terms.label: Cluster
terms.definition: Several networked machines provide a shared pool of computing resources. Page 2 illustrates a seven-machine example.

terms.label: Cluster manager
terms.definition: The resource-allocation component in the example. The illustrated YARN manager supplies requested CPU and memory resources.

terms.label: Container
terms.definition: A resource allocation on a worker node, shown in this YARN example as a specified amount of CPU and memory.

terms.label: Driver
terms.definition: The coordinating process in the illustrated application: it requests executors, schedules work and receives results.

terms.label: Executor
terms.definition: A worker-side process that carries out scheduled tasks. Page 2 follows tasks from the driver to three executors and back.

terms.label: PySpark
terms.definition: The Python interface shown connecting Python code to Spark's JVM-based engine. Page 2 also depicts Python processes beside executor JVMs for Python-side work.

terms.label: Cluster mode
terms.definition: The deployment illustration places the driver inside the cluster rather than on the submitting computer.

terms.label: Client mode
terms.definition: The deployment illustration places the driver on the submitting computer while executors run on cluster workers.

terms.label: Transformation
terms.definition: An operation such as select, filter or withColumn that contributes a step to the planned computation.

terms.label: Action
terms.definition: An operation that asks Spark to produce a result. The guide uses show, count, collect and saving output as examples.

terms.label: Lazy evaluation
terms.definition: Work is described before it is executed. The word-count example queues operations until an action requests the result.

terms.label: Narrow versus wide
terms.definition: The guide distinguishes operations without a shuffle from operations that redistribute rows across partitions.

terms.label: Shuffle
terms.definition: Redistribution of rows between partitions. The word-count and regional-sales examples bring equal keys together before aggregation.

terms.label: Unresolved logical plan
terms.definition: The first planning representation shown after syntax checking; names still need to be checked against available metadata.

terms.label: Catalog
terms.definition: Metadata about available tables, columns and types, used in the guide's semantic check of a query.

terms.label: Catalyst optimizer
terms.definition: The planning component shown rewriting a logical plan before physical execution alternatives are chosen.

terms.label: Filter pushdown
terms.definition: The illustrated optimization moves filtering toward the data source so fewer unwanted rows need further processing.

terms.label: Projection pushdown
terms.definition: The illustrated optimization limits the columns read to the ones needed by the query.

terms.label: Physical plan
terms.definition: A concrete execution strategy. Page 4 shows alternative physical plans and a cost-based choice before scheduling.

terms.label: DAG scheduler
terms.definition: The scheduler in the guide connects the selected execution plan to jobs containing stages and tasks.

terms.label: Job
terms.definition: The execution work requested by an action. Page 5 follows a collect action through its illustrated sales-data pipeline.

terms.label: Stage
terms.definition: A group of work separated from other groups by shuffle boundaries in the illustrated pipeline.

terms.label: Task
terms.definition: The partition-level unit of execution. Page 5 illustrates parallel work on three partitions.

terms.label: On-heap memory
terms.definition: JVM-managed executor memory. The last page divides it into execution/storage, user and reserved regions.

terms.label: Unified memory
terms.definition: The shared execution-and-storage region shown with a movable boundary and borrowing between the two uses.

terms.label: Off-heap memory
terms.definition: Memory outside the JVM heap, configured separately in the guide. The page discusses it in relation to garbage-collection pressure.

terms.label: Overhead memory
terms.definition: Additional executor-container memory requested for operations outside the main heap, as shown in the last-page diagram.

blocks.text: 6. Parameterization

blocks.text: 7. Monitoring
Monitor hub -> pipeline runs -> activity runs. Rerun from the failed activity, not from the top.

items: Run history is kept 45 days - ship to Log Analytics for longer.

Alert on Failed pipeline runs, and on activity duration for silent stalls.

terms.label: Spread

terms.label: Selectable text
terms.definition: Text stored in a PDF that can be selected and copied. An image-only page does not supply this text; extracting it would require a separate OCR step.

5. Copy Activity
Source dataset in, sink dataset out. Everything else is throughput and fault tolerance.

items.text: - Data Integration Units - cloud copy power, 2-256.
- via blob; required for PolyBase into Synapse.

items: Fault tolerance can skip incompatible rows and log them.

blocks.text: 6. Parameterization
Four scopes, one expression language. Knowing which scope a value lives in is most of the battle.

items: Parameters are set at start and immutable; variables are mutable.
Pass values down with Execute Pipeline, never through globals.

blocks.text: 7. Monitoring
Monitor hub -> pipeline runs -> activity runs. Rerun from the failed activity, not from the top.

items: Run history is kept 45 days - ship to Log Analytics for longer.
Annotations are the only practical way to filter runs at scale.
Alert on Failed pipeline runs, and on activity duration for silent stalls.

blocks.text: 8. Traps Worth Memorising

items: A Lookup activity returns at most 5 000 rows / 4 MB.
ForEach inside ForEach is not allowed - use a child pipeline.
Debug runs use the debug IR and ignore triggers.
Deleting a linked service does not warn about dependent datasets.

blocks.title: Example - expressions
Common trap
blocks.text:
A leading @ makes the whole string an expression; inside a literal use @{...}.
Escape a real @ by doubling it: @@.
@{} inside an @-expression is a string-interpolation error.

blocks.title: Important

Rerun from failed activity preserves the original run id - the rerun shows under the same pipeline run.
Diagnostic settings must be enabled before the run, not after.
